newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Search resumes for missing Indian Ocean sheep ship.
newsitem.headline: Search resumes for missing Indian Ocean sheep ship.

text.p: The Indian Ocean search for a burning abandoned ship with almost 70,000 live sheep onboard entered its second day on Saturday with rescue ships following ocean currents in the hope of finding the ship still adrift.
Maritime officials would not speculate on whether the ship had sunk, but said there was no evidence in the search area that the ship had broken up.

Australian maritime officials and Lloyd's shipping service in London said the search was continuing for the missing 14,990 tonne Panama-flagged Uniceb, which has not been heard from since Monday when its crew abandoned ship near the Seychelles after a fire broke out in the engine room.
A rescue tug and converted car carrier were on Saturday following ocean currents in their search but had not had any visual, radar or radio contact since reaching the area on Friday.
"They are proceeding down the anticipated northwest drift of the vessel and hopefully they will pick up the ship that way," a spokesman for Lloyd's in London told Reuters.
The Uniceb left Fremantle in the state of Western Australia on August 23 on a routine 16-day run with 67,000 live sheep bound for Australia's biggest live sheep market, Jordan.
But 400 km (245 miles) east of the Seychelles off the north African coast an engine room fire quickly spread to the crew's quarters, killing one of the ship's 55 crew members.
The remaining crew of 22 Filipinos, 17 Chileans and 15 Indians abandoned ship and were picked up by a passing cargo ship. The Uniceb is owned by Lugano-based firm Sistrin Services.

Australian Maritime Safety Authority spokesman David Gray on Saturday described the situation as "a tragedy", adding that full details of what happened to the ship would not be known until the crew's rescue ship reached the port of Suez on Wednesday.
The missing Uniceb threatens to be Australia's worst live sheep disaster, even though the number of sheep on board is far less than the maximum normal shipment of 120,000.
In 1980, 40,600 sheep were lost in a fire on board a ship travelling from the Australian island state of Tasmania to Iran.
The Uniceb incident has caused a furore in Australia, with animal welfare groups and unionists calling for an end to the live trade.
But livestock officials and politicians are adamant that the trade is worth too much to close it down.

Australian live sheep and cattle exports have grown over the past three decades and are worth about A$500 million (US$395 million) a year. Australia exported 5.54 million live sheep last year, most to the Middle East, worth A$208 million.
